name: Gaussian, Inc.
origin_detail: Gaussian 70 was released in 1970 by John Pople's group at Carnegie Mellon University and distributed through the Quantum Chemistry Program Exchange (QCPE). It was later licensed out of Carnegie Mellon, and since 1987 has been developed and licensed by Gaussian, Inc. Current version Gaussian 16 (2017).
openness_notes: Initial score reflects academic distribution of Gaussian 70 through QCPE before commercial licensing (QCPE terms not reviewed; low confidence). Today it is proprietary: licensees can buy source or binary licences, but the licence bars researchers who develop competing software from using it, and source is not public.

relicensing_events.from: Academic QCPE distribution / Carnegie Mellon licensing
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Commercialisation sustained development for decades; open competitors (e.g. GAMESS, NWChem, Psi4) and commercial rivals (Q-Chem, ORCA licensing) grew alongside it.

risk_events: 'Banned by Gaussian' controversy: the licence bars researchers who develop competing software; an anonymous site, bannedbygaussian.org, listed scientists and institutions it said were barred.
2000: in a WATOC referendum, 23 of 28 executive board members opposed such restrictive licences.

2004: Nature news coverage of the bans (Nature 429, 231). Gaussian's president Michael Frisch called the claim that whole universities are refused 'an outright lie' and said only the competing group is excluded (response page last updated 27 Feb 2014).
No major new version since Gaussian 16 (2017) was found.
robustness: Single private vendor controls the code; users cannot fork it, and competitors' groups can be excluded. Long commercial continuity (since 1987) and a large installed base in chemistry, but scientific reproducibility depends on licence access.
physical_science_relevance: One of the most widely used quantum-chemistry packages in chemistry and molecular materials science; the commercial reference for molecular DFT and ab initio methods.
openness_effect_assessment: Closing the code in 1987 created a durable licence business, but the exclusion of competing developers made Gaussian a long-running symbol of how closed scientific software can restrict benchmarking and critique, prompting a WATOC protest and Nature coverage. No source found quantifies whether the restrictions shifted users to other codes.
key_takeaway: Gaussian shows the sharpest governance risk of closed scientific software: the vendor can decide who may use, test and compare its code, and did so against competing method developers. It is long-lived and commercially stable at modest academic prices ($2,500 to $6,000 per US academic licence), but its licence terms, not its science, are what the community remembers.
